title: The first pledge of Aqaba
hookLine: twelve pledge not to steal, lie, kill their children or slander

cards: A year goes by. The pilgrimage comes round again, and so do the men from Yathrib: twelve of them this time, Ibn Ishaq says.
They meet the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at the same spot, Aqaba, a narrow pass on the edge of Mina, away from the crowds. They've had a year at home to talk, to argue, to wonder.
Now they've come back with their hands out. Not to ask for anything. To give their word.
Today: the first pledge of Aqaba.

teach.b: What did they promise? Ubada ibn al-Samit, whom the sirah names among the twelve, gives the terms in Sahih al-Bukhari.

The Prophet said: pledge to me that you will not set up any partner with God, that you will not steal, that you will not commit adultery, that you will not kill your children, that you will not bring a slander you have invented between your hands and feet, and that you will not disobey me in what is right.
Whoever keeps it, his reward is with God. Look at that list.
No army, no money, no promise to fight for anyone. It's about how they will live: their hands, their tongues, their homes, their children.

Ibn Ishaq says this kind of pledge came to be called the pledge of women, and that it carried no promise of war. The Qur'an, in surah sixty, describes believing women pledging much the same things to the Prophet.
And there's a mercy built in. In Ubada's report the Prophet adds: whoever falls into any of these and is punished in this world, that is an expiation.
And whoever falls and God covers it, it is up to God, to forgive or to punish. The pledge is clear, and realistic.
It expects people to be tested, and it doesn't throw them away when they stumble.
The twelve go home carrying a promise about conduct. Not yet a promise of protection. That comes later.

how: Muslims remember the first pledge of Aqaba as a promise about how to live, and the same list of conduct appears in the Qur'an's description of women pledging to the Prophet.

games.why: a pledge of conduct: no partner with God, no theft, no adultery, no killing children, no slander, and obedience in what is right.

practice: The twelve didn't promise to be good in general; they named things. So name one line you want to keep, from the story's list or your own, and say it to yourself in a single plain sentence, the kind you could actually keep.
If you pray, you can place it before God.

wordCard.voice: Aqaba, the narrow pass where twelve men of Yathrib pledged the Prophet a way of living, not a war. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a pledge of allegiance, given hand in hand.

carryVoice: Your line: a pledge of conduct. Clear enough to keep, with room for anyone who stumbles. Until tomorrow.
